questions.question: Which limit condition is sufficient for $y = L$ to be a horizontal asymptote?
questions.explanation: A finite tail limit $f(x)\to L$ as $x\to+\infty$ makes the graph approach $y=L$.
questions.source_support: The definition says $y = L$ is a horizontal asymptote if the limit at $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ equals $L$.
option_explanations: A finite-point limit is not tail behaviour.

$f(L)=0$ specifies a zero of $f$ at the finite input $L$. The asymptote condition depends instead on a tail limit $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$ or $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L$, which says nothing about the value $f(L)$.

$f'(L)=0$ is a stationary-point condition on the derivative at one finite input. A horizontal asymptote is governed by the tail limit $\lim_{x\to\pm\infty}f(x)=L$, which is independent of the derivative value $f'(L)$.

The function must have a vertical tangent.
The function approaches a constant as the input grows large
questions.explanation: A horizontal asymptote records approach to a constant output along at least one infinite tail.

questions.question: Which statement best reflects the definition of horizontal asymptote?
options: Both limits must exist and both must equal $L$.
One limit at $+\infty$ or $-\infty$ equal to $L$ suffices
questions.explanation: The line $y=L$ is a horizontal asymptote if either $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$ or $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L$; one tail limit suffices.

option_explanations: Both tails need not match; $e^x$ has horizontal asymptote $y=0$ as $x\to-\infty$ while $\lim_{x\to+\infty}e^x=+\infty$ (no finite asymptote), so only one tail has a horizontal asymptote.

$f(0)=L$ fixes the value at the single input $x=0$. The definition requires only a tail limit $\lim_{x\to+\infty}f(x)=L$ or $\lim_{x\to-\infty}f(x)=L$ and imposes no condition on $f(0)$; the asymptote need not even be attained.
Monotonicity is unnecessary; a non-monotone function such as $\sin x/x$ can have a horizontal asymptote $y=0$ as $x\to\pm\infty$.
